1.0.0.en: "The words of the Preacher (Qoheleth), the son of David, king in Jerusalem [1].

1.0.1.en: He is Solomon. Although he did not identify himself by name, he is the son of David, the king in Jerusalem, who, because of his wealth, his wisdom and his worldwide concern in that day, had a great opportunity to test temporal life and to offer this experience to all mankind. We note here:

1.0.2.en: a. He concealed his name "Solomon," which means "peace," because sin had shattered his inner peace and brought troubles upon himself and upon his kingdom, just as it shattered his peace with God, so that he no longer deserved this name. It is as though he were saying, "Do not call me a man of peace, but call me bitter" (Ruth 1:20).

1.0.3.en: b. He called himself "the Preacher" (the Gatherer), because God had gathered him through repentance into His holy flock after he had strayed like a lost sheep; now He brings him back from his wandering to the holy Church through reconciliation with God. Or because he offers his experience and practical wisdom to mankind, so that all may return to the catholic Church. As for his use of the feminine form [the Preacher], perhaps it was a rebuke to himself, since he clung to foreign women and because of them turned aside to idol worship.

1.0.4.en: c. He mentions David's fatherhood to him in order to rebuke himself: that he, the son of that great saint, the author of the Psalms, had wandered and gone astray. And perhaps also to stir hope within himself, for his father David had fallen and risen again, and by his rising from sin he urged many to repentance.

1.0.5.en: d. "King in Jerusalem": he sinned against God, who made him king and did not let him lack anything. What multiplies his sin is that he reigned over the holy city of God, Jerusalem.

1.1.1.en: Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.

1.1.2.en: What profit hath a man of all his labour which he taketh under the sun?" [2-3].

1.1.3.en: The word "vanity" in Hebrew, hebel, basically means "breath" (Isa 57:13) or "vapor," as though the whole world apart from God were like a breath that goes out of a man's nose or a vapor that comes from his mouth on a cold day; he can no longer hold it or be occupied with it, because it quickly disperses into the air.

1.1.4.en: By the word vanity he means that the world is temporal and passing, and that it is without profit in the long run of eternity. Here it is not a solitary monk who offers us his experience and thoughts, but a rich and influential king, with experience in every aspect of life of that time... a realistic and practical discourse.

1.1.5.en: The author affirmed in more than one place that everything in the world is good and useful as a gift of God, but man's misuse of it made it vain, since "the mind itself became vain" (Eph 4:17).

1.1.6.en: He does not push us toward a spirit of despair, but demands of us that our thoughts not be absorbed in earthly and temporal things, and that they not become a goal for us in our worship. In other words, life in all its aspects has no meaning and no benefit, being shallow and passing, unless it is truly bound to God; then, and only then, when it rests on God and on His word, does it have value.

1.1.7.en: * Why are you bound by the love of temporary things?

1.1.8.en: Why do you run after the things that hold the last place, as though they had the first priority, though they are vain and a lie? For you want them to dwell with you, while they pass away like a shadow.

1.1.9.en: St. Augustine * Calls everything we see and struggle for, as a visible reality, "vanity."

1.1.10.en: What is vain lacks "substance," and what lacks "substance" carries no power!

1.1.11.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa * "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity." Let us go to the tombs; show me your father, show me your wife. Where is the one who wore gilded garments? The one who rode in the chariot? The one who had armies, who had a girdle of office, and who had heralds? The one who killed these and cast those into prison? Who put to death whom he would and pardoned whom he would? I see nothing but bones, worms and spiders' webs. All these are dust, weakness, a dream, a shadow, a mere (frail) relation and an image, indeed not even reaching the level of an image.

1.1.12.en: St. John Chrysostom The aim of affirming the vanity of this world is to train the heart not to hate the world but rather to love heaven and to enjoy God the Word, as the Eternal One who satisfies the soul:

1.1.13.en: * "All is vanity, saith the Preacher," everything in this world. Therefore whoever desires salvation, let him rise above the world and seek the "Word" who is with God, fleeing from this world and leaving the earth. For no one can grasp what exists always unless he first flees from here. For this reason also, when the Lord wished to draw near to God the Father (who is one with Him), He said to His disciples, "Arise, let us go hence" (Jn 14:31).

1.1.14.en: St. Ambrose * [In the words of the Lord Christ, the Word of God who satisfies the soul]

1.1.15.en: I am your father, your brother, your bridegroom, your house, your garment, your source and your foundation.

1.1.16.en: I am everything you long for; so you will lack nothing.

1.1.17.en: I will be your servant, for I came to serve, not to be served.

1.1.18.en: I am your friend, your member, your head, your brother, your sister, your mother, and everything to you... only be a friend to me...

1.1.20.en: Why do you turn away the One who loves you?

1.1.21.en: Why do you toil for this world?

1.1.22.en: Why do you draw water with a leaking vessel, for such is toil for the present life?

1.1.23.en: Why do you spin wool in the fire?

1.1.24.en: Why do you wrestle with the air?

1.1.25.en: Why do you run in vain?

1.1.26.en: Does not every art have a purpose? This is plain to all; but you are without aim. Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.

1.1.27.en: * Let us believe Him and hold fast to the things in which there is nothing vain, but only what is true; what is founded on solid rock, where there is no old age and no decline, but everything is flourishing and fresh, without corruption, aging or dissolution.

1.1.28.en: I ask you that we love God with a sincere affection, not for fear of hell, but out of desire for the Kingdom.

1.1.29.en: What can be compared to seeing Christ? Certainly nothing!

1.1.30.en: What delight shall we obtain from these good things...? "Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him" (1 Cor 2:9).

1.1.31.en: St. John Chrysostom * It is not one who has become a companion of the angels and has grown familiar with their mysteries and has not despised the company of the world.

1.1.32.en: * If you leave your possessions for His sake, you will possess Him in yourself forever.

1.1.33.en: How sweet is the departure of those who love You to You, O Physician, and how hard is the departure of the lovers of the world from it, because those move on to their inheritance, while these depart from what is theirs.

1.1.34.en: * Who is this who has tasted the sweetness of the fruits of the tree of life and wants to run after the foul fruits of the world?!

1.1.35.en: St. John Saba The question that many have raised: Why is the world called vain when it was made by God, who is all good? In other words: does the good God create something without benefit?

1.1.36.en: God sees that everything He created is "good" (Gen 1:10, 12, 18, 31); but man, whose mind, nature and inner insight were corrupted, wronged his view of the world as he wronged his use of it, so the world became vain. The world, which is God's handiwork, is good; it was created for man, that he might work in it and rejoice... But now that man has been shattered in his nature, the world no longer fulfills its purpose as his servant.

1.1.37.en: * If (creation) is the works of God, how can it be vain? The dispute over this matter is great. But hear, beloved: it is not the works of God that we call vain, God forbid! The heaven is not vain; the earth is not vain, God forbid! Neither the sun nor the moon nor the stars, nor our bodies. No! For all these are very good (Gen 1:31).

1.1.38.en: What, then, is the vain thing? Let us hear the Preacher himself, when he says, "I planted vineyards for myself; I got me men singers and women singers; I made me pools of water; and I had possessions of herds and flocks; I gathered me also silver and gold; and I saw that all these were vanity" (cf. Eccl 2:4-8). And he says, "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity" (Eccl 12:8). Hear also what the prophet says: "He heapeth up riches, and knoweth not who shall gather them" (Ps 39:6). Such is vain: your magnificent buildings, your excessive wealth, the crowd of slaves jostling in the public square, your vain glory and pomp, your haughty thoughts and your boasting; all these are vain, for they are not from the hand of God but are from your own doing. And why are they vain? Because they have no useful end.

1.1.39.en: St. John Chrysostom St. John Chrysostom speaks to us, in his treatise "No one can harm a man unless he harms himself," about the concept of goodness at some length, explaining that the world with all that is in it is neither good nor evil in itself, but man's use of it turns it to good or to evil. Whoever uses money for evil, it becomes evil to him; and whoever supports his needy brethren with it, it becomes a blessing to him, and so on...

1.1.40.en: Finally, St. Augustine sees that it befits the believer to transfer his temporal possessions to the true life through almsgiving, saying: [We must hold fast to the true life, so let us transfer our wealth to the place of the true life, and there we shall find what we gave here. He (God) accomplishes this transfer of our possessions, He who wrought the change in our souls]. The Lord Christ, who has seated us in the heavenlies, transfers our money to heaven!

1.2.0.en: Although man, by the corruption of his nature, mind and inner insight, has made the world vain, man remains in God's eyes more precious than the whole world! "What is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?" (Mt 16:26). For God created the world for man, not man for the world. Therefore it befits man in his striving and labor, whether in his private life, his family life, his work or his worship, not to turn his gaze away from his inner life and its satisfaction in God Himself. For this reason the Preacher warns us against every striving in which man loses his goal, saying, "What profit hath a man of all his labour which he taketh under the sun?!" [3]. Our labor in our daily life and in our worship will not be able to satisfy the soul, atone for its sin, heal its wounds and sanctify it, unless we lean on the Savior's breast by practical faith and ask for the work of His Holy Spirit in us.

1.2.1.en: * Man's righteousness is counted as nothing. The work of men, what is it? All their labor is vain.

1.2.2.en: From You, O Lord, and by Your grace our nature becomes good. From You is righteousness; so we men become righteous. From You are mercy and grace. So we are changed from dust into Your image.

1.2.3.en: Give strength to our will, so that we may not sink into sin.

1.2.4.en: St. Ephrem the Syrian As long as we are "under the sun," we are subject to trials and suffer from its heat (Mt 20:12). And we shall gain nothing from all our labor; but if we receive the Sun of Righteousness within us, He lifts us above every evil trial, and the flame of passions cannot touch our inner depths. The Sun of Righteousness bears us up by His Holy Spirit so that the soul may enjoy the pledge of eternal glory, and we say, "He made us sit together with Him in the heavenly places" (Eph 2:6).

1.2.5.en: * By "labor" here [3] he points to the life of the flesh, which seeks no profit in any good work. It says, "What profit hath a man?", that is, what does the soul gather from all the labor of life, in the life of those who live only for luxuries.

1.3.0.en: 4 One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever. 5 The sun also ariseth, and the sun goeth down, and hasteth to his place where he arose. 6 The wind goeth toward the south, and turneth about unto the north; it whirleth about continually, and the wind returneth again according to his circuits. 7 All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full; unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again. 8 All speech falls short. Man cannot declare it all. The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing. 9 The thing that hath been, it is that which shall be; and that which is done is that which shall be done: and there is no new thing under the sun. 10 If anything is found of which it is said, "See, this is new!" it was already of old time, in the ages which were before us. 11 There is no remembrance of former things; neither shall there be any remembrance of things that are to come with those that shall come after.

1.3.1.en: The Preacher offers real examples from nature that confirm the brevity of temporal life, its changing nature and its inability to satisfy the heart; that there is truly nothing new in life despite progress and development; and finally, that whatever honor or desire man attains, time wipes out by forgetfulness.

1.4.s.en: a. The brevity of human life:

1.4.0.en: "One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever" [4].

1.4.1.en: The Preacher shows that the period of our enjoyment of earthly things is extremely short. For although the earth was created for man and for his comfort, man lives in a generation that ends with him, to be replaced by another generation, while the earth remains until the end of the age.

1.4.2.en: * The mortal remains mortal, whether honored or not honored... The wise Preacher says, "The earth abideth for ever," serving every generation, the first and the next that is born after it upon it; but men... come into life by the will of their Creator without knowing it, and are taken from it before they wish it. And yet, in spite of this extreme vanity, they think they are the masters of the earth.

1.5.s.en: b. The changing nature of all beings:

1.5.0.en: Everything in the world changes; the sun rises and sets, then returns and rises... and so the movement never stops. The position of the earth in relation to the sun changes, so that sunrise and sunset occur, which is repeated daily.

1.5.1.en: So also the winds move in certain courses; and the waters also move, as they evaporate and become clouds, then rain, then rivers, and return to the seas and oceans to evaporate again!

1.5.2.en: Our looking at nature and the changes it contains, which touch all beings, reveals to us the nature of the world, that it is not stable but ever changing, and therefore will not remain forever. It is as though it does not befit man, who carries within him a natural longing for immortality, to attach himself to what is changing and passing away.

1.5.3.en: And perhaps the author wanted to show that man, for whose sake nature moves before him, the beings such as the stars, the winds and the clouds, is himself helpless; what is in his hand?!

1.5.4.en: And perhaps he also wanted to declare that nature itself changes, the sunrise being followed by sunset and then sunrise again, and so on... while man is unable to move; he is born, then dies and does not rise again upon the same earth! How great is man, for whose sake this universe exists with all its known and hidden powers and laws, and how weak he is, for it is hard for him to change even his inner nature?! Man is great in God, who gives him everything, and exceedingly weak in himself alone!

1.5.5.en: * We see in the sun a symbol of the rising and setting of our nature. There is one road for all, there is one circle for everyone in the journey of life. By birth we rise, then we descend again to our natural place. And when we reach the sunset of life, our light sinks down below the earth... What is of the earth dissolves completely into its element, and the circle continues on its way again and again.

1.6.2.en: The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing" [8].

1.6.3.en: Can we expect satisfaction for a soul made in the image of God from temporal, passing things full of toil?! For nature, with all its resources, cannot satisfy even the senses of sight, hearing or smell, so how can it satisfy the inner life?!

1.6.4.en: * We wake every day to eat and drink, and yet no one is satisfied so as not to hunger or thirst again shortly.

1.6.5.en: We seek gain every day, and greed has no limits!

1.6.6.en: "The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing." He that loveth silver is not satisfied with silver.

1.6.7.en: There is no limit to toil, and no profit in wealth.

1.7.s.en: d. There is nothing new in creation:

1.7.0.en: With all the wealth, increasing pleasures, fame and glory that the Preacher obtained, he realized that there is nothing new under the sun. True, outward circumstances and man's capabilities develop, but his nature, and also his feelings and motives, remain as they have been since the first man was created. What aroused the instinct of the young man in the last century may be loathed by the young man of today, but the nature of the instincts in a young man's life remains the same through the ages, even if the form of the stimulus differs. Everything under the sun has not changed; what is new is what is above the sun, that is, the enjoyment of the new life we have in Christ Jesus, the Sun of Righteousness, and we hear Him say, "Behold, I make all things new" (Rev 21:5). We say with the Apostle Paul: "Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new" (2 Cor 5:17).

1.7.1.en: Man often feels the need for renewal... He seeks what is new merely because it is new, and rejects what is old merely because it is old. This feeling springs from an inner need that touches the very being of his nature, but instead of renewing his nature by the Spirit of God, he seeks an outward renewal or change, such as new models, new theories and new expressions. So you find modern man wanting, if possible, to renew everything around him, not only his work, his house, his city or his car, but sometimes his husband or wife... He feels a measure of boredom and seeks renewal!

1.7.2.en: The soul that is united to the Lord Christ as its Bridegroom is led by the Holy Spirit to continual renewal in inward thought, so it feels no boredom or weariness, but lives rejoicing in the Spirit as in heaven, untouched by old age and unaffected by aging.

1.7.3.en: * Because God is perfect, He became perfect man, and entered with all that is new into perfection; this is the only new thing under the sun, through which He declared the riches of God's surpassing power!

1.8.s.en: e. Forgetfulness is the mark of every age:

1.8.0.en: "There is no remembrance of former things; neither shall there be any remembrance of things that are to come with those that shall come after" [11].

1.8.1.en: Man lives longing to immortalize his memory or the memory of his family, but the world forgets the former ones, and we who are the latter will be forgotten by the coming generations. What, then, is the profit to man if he concentrates his labor on acquiring the wealth or glory of the world? Wealth passes away, and glory is forgotten! Even mere remembrance, time is able to destroy.

1.9.0.en: 12 I the Preacher was king over Israel in Jerusalem. 13 And I gave my heart to seek and search out by wisdom concerning all things that are done under heaven: this sore travail hath God given to the sons of man to be exercised therewith. 14 I have seen all the works that are done under the sun; and, behold, all is vanity and vexation of spirit. 15 That which is crooked cannot be made straight: and that which is wanting cannot be numbered. 16 I communed with mine own heart, saying, Lo, I am come to great estate, and have gotten more wisdom than all they that have been before me in Jerusalem: yea, my heart had great experience of wisdom and knowledge. 17 And I gave my heart to know wisdom, and to know madness and folly: I perceived that this also is vexation of spirit. 18 For in much wisdom is much grief: and he that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow.

1.9.1.en: The Preacher presented proofs from the reality of nature concerning the vanity of the world: its passing away, its instability, and its inability to satisfy the inner man or to renew corrupt human nature, showing that time takes from man even the fame or glory for which he spared no effort. Now, being a great king who lacks nothing, he pursues human wisdom, examining by wisdom what goes on in the world so as to have knowledge and learning... and behold, he arrives at a negative experience that does not satisfy.

1.9.2.en: a. "I the Preacher was king over Israel in Jerusalem.

1.9.3.en: And I gave my heart to seek and search out by wisdom concerning all things that are done under heaven" [12-13].

1.10.0.en: He set his heart to seek and search out by wisdom, instead of lifting his heart to God to ask for heavenly wisdom (Jas 1:5). He needed to enter into dialogue with God, who alone gives constructive heavenly wisdom, instead of dialogue with himself outside the circle of God, to obtain human wisdom that is unable to satisfy his soul... "For in much wisdom is much grief: and he that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow" [18].

1.10.1.en: The wisdom of God reveals our weaknesses, but it gives us hope and offers us possibilities for work; whereas human wisdom, though it shows the weaknesses, leads us into grief and despair: Who will renew my nature, whose corruption I have discovered? Who can set right my inner and outer circumstances? Who will move the world for my edification? The Preacher says, "That which is crooked cannot be made straight, and that which is wanting cannot be numbered" [15]... a bitter feeling of complete inability to set things right.

1.10.2.en: * The stubborn man cannot become virtuous (by his wisdom), nor the corrupt man become respected... We can also understand this verse [15] thus: there is such great evil in this world that it is hard to return to the original state of right order. It is not easy to return to what (man) was in his first creation, in perfection and order; but through repentance everything can be restored to uprightness, though Satan remains resistant in his error.

1.10.3.en: St. Jerome Here it befits us to distinguish between recourse to human wisdom alone, relying on bare human experience, and the sanctification of human thought and human experience by the work of God. For this reason we are not surprised to see St. Clement of Alexandria believe that there is no enmity between faith and philosophy; the latter is not a work of darkness as some suppose, but carries a partial truth, which needs perfecting and purifying from all the impurities that entered into it, through the work of faith. As for the Fathers who attacked human wisdom, they attacked only reliance on it outside the circle of God.

1.10.4.en: * In my opinion every sensible man thinks that learning is the chief of all that is good... We must keep what can help us to contemplate the truth, avoiding everything that leads to evil, error and destruction.

1.10.5.en: * It is necessary to use discernment in education, in such a way that we choose useful learning and avoid everything harmful and ominous.

1.10.6.en: * We must begin by reading worldly thought in order to rise afterward to the holy things and the mysteries of the faith... If there is agreement between this culture and our doctrines, knowing it is of great benefit; and if not, the comparison in the opposite case will confirm our correct beliefs.

1.10.7.en: St. Basil the Great Let us seek the wisdom that is mixed with humility and agrees with the spirit of faith; but the wisdom that springs from man's pride, his self-reliance and his separation from his Creator is a hindrance... The Fathers call it "the wisdom of this world."

1.10.8.en: * No one is wise in knowledge except the one who has put away from himself the wisdom of this world.

1.10.9.en: * Despise your wisdom and reject it, that the wisdom of the Lord may dwell in you.

1.10.10.en: St. John Saba b. If God gave man a longing to seek wisdom and to search into all things, this wisdom revealed to the Preacher that the life God gave him is a sore travail [13]; for many ask: Why did God place us in a world full of misery?

1.10.11.en: God did not create us to live in a world of misery and toil, but the misuse of the world and the wrong view of it corrupted our life and distorted the image of the world in our eyes.

1.10.12.en: "I have seen all the works that are done under the sun; and, behold, all is vanity and vexation (a seizing) of spirit" [14].

1.10.13.en: What does "vexation of spirit" (a seizing of the wind) mean? Some translate it "wrestling with the wind" or "feeding on the wind," that is, that feeding on food is of no value, like the wind; or that the soul in its hunger grasps everything around it in the world to eat it, and behold, it eats wind. This points to the loss of purpose in human activities, their barrenness, and their inability to give true satisfaction within man, or inner reform and healing. St. Augustine sees that the seizing of the wind points to the vain pride into which man falls by seeking temporary things.

1.10.14.en: This is what the Preacher reached through the wisdom and knowledge he received as king of Israel, and the neighboring peoples were accustomed to say, "This great nation is a wise and understanding people" (Deut 4:6). And Solomon was known for wisdom, as he says: "I communed with mine own heart, saying, Lo, I am come to great estate, and have gotten more wisdom than all they that have been before me in Jerusalem: yea, my heart had great experience of wisdom and knowledge" [16].

1.10.15.en: c. The Preacher offers us his experience as he pursues wisdom, learning and knowledge, the greatest things in the world, "for in much wisdom is much grief: and he that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow" [18]. Here he does not attack wisdom or learning, but declares their inability to bring happiness and joy to man. For by wisdom and learning, as we said before, man discovers his need of many things he cannot attain, and so he is filled with sorrow. As St. Augustine says: [Whenever I long for much and do not find it here, does not my sorrow for it increase the more until it is fulfilled? Do I not weep the more until what I seek is accomplished?!]. He also says: [By obtaining this knowledge he gains sorrow also, because of his inability to fulfil the desire to reach his fitting homeland, his Creator and his blessed God]. And St. Gregory of Nazianzus says: [Solomon says: I said, I will be wise; but it was far from me. Truly he who increases in knowledge increases in grief. For the joy that springs from what we discover is not greater than the pain because of what (we do not obtain but) escapes us; it is a pain that I imagine like that felt by those who are drawn up from the waters while thirsty, or those who are unable to reach what they think they are holding, or one who is suddenly left in darkness by the burst of a swift flash of light].

1.10.16.en: This is the work of wisdom, the greatest thing we possess here; what, then, are the rest of the things of the world? We need the "wisdom of God," who alone is able to satisfy the soul, not temporal, earthly wisdom.

1.10.17.en: "Howbeit we speak wisdom among them that are perfect: yet not the wisdom of this world, nor of the princes of this world, that come to nought: but we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom, which God ordained before the world unto our glory" (1 Cor 2:6-7).

1.10.18.en: "But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption" (1 Cor 1:30).

1.10.19.en: Therefore let us possess our Christ within us; He is the true wisdom, and He alone is able to save our souls, satisfy them, make them grow and glorify them!
